entry.title: Post-Quantum Perfect Zero-Knowledge Arguments for NP From Any One-Way Permutation
entry.summary: In this paper, we show for the first time that post-quantum one-way permutations are sufficient for perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for all of NP with security guaranteed against quantum adversaries. We first establish that Naor, Ostrovsky,Venkatesen, and Yung's bit commitment scheme built from any permutation using interactive hashing, called the NOVY scheme, is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum polynomial-time committers provided the permutation is post-quantum one-way. We then show that the collapse-binding property of the NOVY scheme allows for Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE to remain so exactly as it stands against quantum adversaries.

entry.title: Spoofing the Toolbox: Optimizing Tool Descriptions to Deceive LLM Agents
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are widely used in many applications and often rely on external tools. Tool information, such as function descriptions, helps agents determine which tools best suit a given context. However, attackers can manipulate this information to mislead LLM agents into using malicious tools. Prior attacks mainly rely on keyword-based techniques, which are easily detected, or rule-based methods, which have limited effectiveness. In this work, we introduce TSA, a stealthy tool-spoofing attack that crafts descriptions for malicious tools that are difficult to distinguish from those of existing benign tools. To achieve this, we propose an LLM-powered optimization method that iteratively refines malicious tool descriptions. Specifically, TSA begins with a variant of a benign tool description and updates it based on feedback from a surrogate LLM agent. The optimization method incorporates a feedback function and contrastive in-context learning to guide the search for descriptions that are both stealthy and effective. Experiments on both single- and multi-tool use benchmarks demonstrate that TSA achieves an attack success rate of up to 92.13\%, outperforming four state-of-the-art approaches while remaining highly stealthy. Our user study further shows that even human participants cannot distinguish descriptions generated by TSA from benign ones. Moreover, TSA remains effective against five tool-malware detectors.

entry.title: STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
entry.summary: We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.
entry.arxiv:comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, and 16 pages of Supplementary Information with 3 figures and 5 tables

entry.title: EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
entry.summary: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.

entry.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
entry.summary: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.

entry.title: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
entry.summary: The consensus protocols of most high-performance blockchains use quorum certificates, which bundle the signatures of a quorum of validators. Signature schemes such as BLS can aggregate the signatures of a whole quorum into a single short signature, which keeps these certificates small. A large-scale quantum computer would break these schemes, and no post-quantum scheme with comparable aggregate size and aggregation time is known. Without aggregation, a certificate holds one large post-quantum signature per member of the quorum, so it becomes infeasible for each validator to broadcast certificates, as modern consensus protocols often require. We present Quantum Cadence, a post-quantum consensus protocol with multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates altogether: every validator counts quorums among the messages it has received itself. Its safety and liveness do not even depend on signatures, although we add signatures to obtain accountability. Quantum Cadence builds on Cadence and replaces its slot consensus, Chorus, with Quantum Chorus, which keeps the optimal fast-path latency of Chorus: dissemination followed by two rounds of votes. When its fast path fails, Quantum Chorus runs Coda, our signature-free Byzantine agreement for multiple proposers. We also outline how the Conductor, which schedules the slots of Cadence, can be adapted to Quantum Cadence. In simulations with 200 validators, Quantum Chorus has a latency comparable to that of Chorus and scales better with the number of proposers.

entry.title: Developing Security Metrics for Automated Compliance Checking
entry.summary: To automatically check for compliance with security-related standards, prose requirements must be translated to technical properties to make them measurable. A multitude of metrics have been proposed in past literature, but they are lacking a systematic methodology for their elicitation. Without such a methodology, metrics remain inconsistent in their data models and abstraction levels, they exhibit considerable overlaps and are difficult to combine to comprehensively cover a standard's requirement. In this paper, we develop a data model for security metrics based on a systematization of compliance requirements, and we propose a methodology for their elicitation. The method is based on an ontology that enables a systematic development of metrics with a comparable degree of abstraction. We also present our initial work on an open-source effort that demonstrates that our approach also supports a collaborative development of metrics.

entry.title: Identity Amortization: Shared Resources and the Cost of Sybil Attacks
entry.summary: Sybil defenses commonly price identities by requiring a resource for each one. When one resource can support several identities, an adversary can pay less per identity than the defense intends. We call this identity amortization: a strict reduction in the minimum cost of provisioning identities when resources may be shared, relative to provisioning each one independently. It is a second route to the gap that a Sybil attack exploits. When influence is assigned per identity, a defense calibrated to the nominal price can overestimate the cost of a Sybil threshold by up to the number of identities one resource supports. For any resource catalogue, we give exact tests for when identity amortization occurs, where it begins, and its largest error; a sharing cap below the onset removes it. Because the tests need only prices and capacities, they apply to any defense that admits identities against a shareable resource, telling designers whether the assumed per-identity cost is paid, how wrong it can be, and which intervention restores it most cheaply for honest participants. On published phone-verification prices, per-account estimates overstate provisioning cost 1.6 to 4.3 times; Tor's raised per-address relay limit cut modeled attack cost by 8 to 72%, depending on the address-to-relay price ratio.

entry.title: Iterative Behavioral Identification for Covert Misappropriation Attacks
entry.summary: We present a data-driven, three-phase framework for covert misappropriation attacks on closed-loop networked control systems. A man-in-the-middle (MITM) adversary, with access only to intercepted input-output data, incrementally identifies the plant's behavioral subspace while maintaining stealth under an infinity-norm intrusion-detection system (IDS). Phase 1 collects an initial rank-deficient Hankel matrix using a low-amplitude probing signal that satisfies an analytical stealth bound. Phase 2 adapts online rank-increasing experiment design to the closed-loop setting, using causal predictor-based masking to limit IDS residuals while the Hankel rank grows from 1 to the full behavioral rank n + mL in exactly n + mL - 1 steps. We show that the identified subspaces are strictly nested and that the projection error of any desired trajectory decreases monotonically, strictly so almost surely at each rank increase. Phase 3 employs the final Hankel matrix in a DeePC-style optimization to synthesize a covert attack that tracks an arbitrary reference while respecting the IDS constraint. Simulations on a DC motor with PI control demonstrate full-rank identification and stealthy tracking. Stealth is guaranteed analytically in Phases 1 and 3 and is numerically supported in Phase 2. The method is model-free and assumes noise-free LTI dynamics.

entry.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection
entry.summary: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35-0.93 depending on the type), leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.

entry.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
entry.summary: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overhead.

entry.title: On Task, Off Track: Benchmarking LLM and Agent Robustness to Near-Target Prompt Injection
entry.summary: Prompt injection benchmarks assess whether large language models (LLMs) and agents resist malicious instructions embedded in external content. However, a system could perform well by rejecting attacks that obviously abandon the user's request, while still accepting changes that retain most of a legitimate answer but make it incorrect or harmful. Testing more instructions for unrelated outcomes would not necessarily reveal this weakness. We call attacks seeking responses designed to resemble legitimate answers while introducing incorrect or harmful changes near-target prompt injection. We introduce NTBench, the Near-Target Benchmark, which builds on legitimate tasks from existing datasets. For each task, a legitimate reference outcome guides the generation of target--instruction pairs, with separate tracks targeting incorrect and harmful outcomes in responses or agent tool invocations. Harmful targets can also accompany otherwise correct task completion. We combine LLM-based checks with human validation of the intended deviations, then assess whether injected instructions induce them using response judgments or tool-call checks, excluding deviations already observed without injection. We evaluate seven LLMs on ten datasets for language tasks and two agent benchmarks. Under a common budget of three attack executions per sample, both tracks achieve higher overall attack success rates than the fixed-target baseline for every evaluated model in each setting. On language tasks, the increases range from 9.3 to 35.8 percentage points for incorrect targets and 1.7 to 17.3 percentage points for harmful targets. These results show that resistance to the tested fixed-target attacks does not imply resistance to related incorrect or harmful outcomes, and that reference-guided targets broaden the failures revealed by robustness evaluation.

entry.title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation
entry.summary: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.

entry.title: Embedding Large PQC KEMs in IKEv2
entry.summary: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms carry public keys far larger than the established VPN handshake protocol IKEv2 was designed for. At the same time, its initial exchange comprising the public keys cannot be fragmented. In response, the IETF discusses a range of protocol adjustments, yet these proposals have never been compared in terms of their performance and stability under identical conditions. We systematically screened the IETF document corpus for such proposals, added three of our own (one using forward error correction and two using IKEv2 with QUIC, namely QUIKE and QUIKE with a composite key exchange), identified two specification gaps in existing acknowledgment drafts, and implemented all eight on the same open-source codebase. Measurements across different bandwidths, latencies, and packet loss rates, and with ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, and Classic McEliece, total 126 500 handshakes in 1296 different configurations and show that no mechanism fully compensates for the effect of the key size on performance. For Classic McEliece, no approach handles challenging conditions acceptably. The approaches either congest the link or take up to nearly two minutes per handshake on average. For ML-KEM and FrodoKEM, there are two ways forward: building on already standardized extensions or delegating the transport. The former requires the larger implementation change and needs further optimization, such as acknowledgment mechanisms or error-correcting codes, but grants continuity and compatibility. The latter can use a composite key exchange to avoid these drawbacks and achieve a faster, more resilient handshake and leaner implementation, with QUIKE-composite offering the best overall performance.

entry.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
entry.summary: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden--either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors--making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework for end-to-end AVR that performs deep analysis by transforming intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. DeepAVR decomposes repair into specialized roles--Fault Localization, Patch Generation, Compile Validation, Security Validation, Functionality Validation, and Patch Review--and routes feedback across these roles to iteratively refine both localization and patch hypotheses. In particular, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, which treats execution results from intermediate patches as diagnostic signals to uncover hidden root causes, and a root-cause-oriented patch review stage that detects symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs beyond execution-based validation. Evaluation on the real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset VulnLoc shows that DeepAVR significantly outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Furthermore, results on SAN2VULN demonstrate strong generalization, with DeepAVR effectively repairing vulnerabilities unseen during training.

entry.title: Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks on Code Models via Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring
entry.summary: Pre-trained code models are exposed to backdoor poisoning, in which crafted training samples make the model misbehave on a trigger. A capable attacker minimizes the number of such samples, since each adds cost and exposure and a lower poisoning rate leaves a smaller footprint for defenses. Which samples to poison therefore matters, but existing data-efficient selection methods target image classification, offer no scoring mechanism for autoregressive generation, and have not been studied on code. We propose Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring (TNCS), which isolates a trigger's contribution to the target behavior by comparing the scoring model's output on a triggered input with its output on a trigger-neutralized counterfactual, covering classification and generation alike. TNCS attains higher attack success rates than the baselines at very low poisoning ratios, across three CodeXGLUE tasks and five trigger families, without degrading clean-task performance, and its margin grows as the ratio decreases. It is the only method effective on every trigger family, and its selected poison set transfers to mismatched victims.

entry.title: Automated Post-Exploitation Attack Chain Exploration Based on a Phase-guided Hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search Algorithm
entry.summary: Advanced attackers in post-exploitation scenarios increasingly craft attack chains that combine benign operations, configuration errors, and vulnerability exploitation to achieve objectives like privilege escalation. While such chains pose significant threats, manually discovering them in complex modern host environments is prohibitively labor-intensive. Automating this discovery is therefore essential for proactive defense, yet existing methods still suffer from inefficiency and lack diversity when exploring these attack chains. To address these limitations, we present APEX, an Automated Post-EXploitation attack chain exploration system. This system transforms attack chain discovery into a planning problem and solves it with a novel phase-guided hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. By organizing attack actions into semantic phases and integrating symbolic planning with MCTS, APEX enables efficient exploration of the state space while generating multiple diverse chains. Evaluations on a benchmark comprising 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems and 291 cloud instances demonstrate that APEX successfully discovers both known and previously unreported attack chains--including 9 novel privilege escalation vectors--providing actionable intelligence for hardening complex production environments.

entry.title: Autonomous Cyber Weapons as AI-Enabled Digital Harms: A Platform Accountability Framework
entry.summary: Governments govern AI-generated online harms from commercial platforms (EU DSA, AI Act, UK Online Safety Act), yet the most severe class remains ungoverned: autonomous cyber weapons (ACWs) deployed by nation-states against civilian infrastructure. We address this gap with three contributions: a digital-harm taxonomy (six ACW modes $\times$ five harm categories); the Meaningful Human Control (MHC) Model, a governance-compliance function with a closed-form IHL threshold and a proved weight-sensitivity bound; and a platform accountability architecture with treaty language grounded in ARSIWA state-responsibility doctrine, not Rome Statute individual responsibility. Applied to eleven documented state-attributed operations and one hypothetical defensive AI system, every documented case falls in an accountability vacuum; the threshold is target-dependent, and against wholly civilian targets no system studied clears it, including the hypothetical. Three further incidents are correctly excluded on autonomy/attribution grounds, a discriminant-validity check. The weights and threshold parameters are illustrative, not fitted.
entry.arxiv:comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Presented at the 2026 IDeaS Conference (Carnegie Mellon University)

entry.title: Democratic Accountability for Autonomous Systems: A Legislative Notification Framework and Comparative Institutional Design
entry.summary: No domestic legislature has ever reviewed a state's decision to authorise an autonomous cyber weapon before it acted. Closing the international attribution gap is necessary but not sufficient for democratic accountability. We formalise the Tripartite Attribution Framework's three attribution levels and add a fourth, non-legal Democratic Accountability level ($A_{dem}$): a 72-hour legislative notification requirement. Scoring six democratic oversight bodies against five adoptability dimensions yields a counter-intuitive result: the statutes granting these bodies privileged access to classified material are often the same statutes withholding particular ongoing operations from them, so at most one could lawfully receive such a notification today, and the carve-out Level 4 needs is required in nearly every jurisdiction rather than only the least-equipped. Retrospective analysis of Stuxnet, NotPetya, and Volt Typhoon shows one pattern: legal attribution resolvable, domestic democratic review absent.
entry.arxiv:comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Presented at the 2026 IDeaS Conference (Carnegie Mellon University)

entry.title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum
entry.summary: Illicit actors exploit Ethereum's deep liquidity and diverse on-chain services to launder criminal proceeds by combining decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers in multi-stage processes. Existing anti-money laundering tracing methods fail to disentangle the underlying asset-flow paths in complex transactions, potentially misdirecting subsequent tracing; cannot identify cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge information; and treat mixers as generic exit services, overlooking post-mixer laundering flows. We present FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets across Ethereum services. First, we propose a method based on the Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to recover intra-transaction asset-flow paths, which guide accurate tracing and service analysis. Second, we extract discriminative features from asset-flow and execution-evidence perspectives and train a classifier to identify transactions with cross-chain intent. Third, we leverage evidence from the upstream laundering network to analyze potential post-mixer laundering activities. Evaluation on 20 real-world laundering cases demonstrates FPTracer's effectiveness. It achieves the highest recall for both known laundering addresses (98.6%) and destinations (94.2%). It identifies all known uses of bridges in these cases and uncovers 30 previously unreported ones. Among 18 cases with identified Tornado Cash usage, FPTracer can identify potential withdrawal-side activities, which are corroborated by public reports where available.

entry.title: The 3DS Oracle: BIN Attack via the Network
entry.summary: EMV 3-D Secure (3DS) requires a client-visible continuation boundary in browser-mediated flows; in some deployments, that boundary exposes a pre-authorization classification channel. This paper studies 3DS as a protocol, integration surface, and governance problem, combining standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history, and a bounded live evaluation. We show that client-visible integrations can reflect routing and authentication state before financial authorization, allowing 3DS to function as a profiling and screening channel for issuer controls and cardholder/account state rather than only as a defense. In the tested browser-channel Braintree/Cardinal path, the first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchor cards from bounded adjacent same-range comparison PANs in six of seven distinct ACS/card-range cohorts; separate public evidence, including openly accessible attacker tooling, rotating-proxy support, and illicit paid 3DS card-testing services, shows that comparable signals are already operationalized in the wild. Our live study was deliberately bounded for ethical reasons, so the empirical ceiling reported here reflects researcher restraint rather than an attacker-side scalability limit, although we do not claim network-wide prevalence or candidate issuance. The deeper issue is systemic: decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-boundary assumptions, identifier-linked routing invariants, and fragmented accountability let the exposure persist even when individual actors appear locally conformant. Meaningful remediation therefore requires consortium-level reform, including stricter minimization of client-visible pre-authorization responses, more uniform continuation behavior, and stronger client authenticity and session binding.

entry.title: Benchmarking Classical and Quantum Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection Across Multiple Datasets
entry.summary: Intrusion detection is examined through a comparative benchmark of classical and quantum machine learning models on three datasets: NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and MQTTEEB-D2025. The analysis focuses on how preprocessing decisions, feature selection strategies, and quantum encoding schemes shape model performance on data with differing levels of noise and complexity. A single unified pipeline is applied, covering normalization, class-imbalance handling, dimensionality reduction, and two feature selection methods: Random Forest importance and a quantum-aware approach that combines Quantum Kernel Alignment with Mutual Information (QKA-MI). Four classifiers are compared: Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, Quantum Support Vector Machine, and Pegasos Quantum SVM. The classical models perform consistently across all three datasets, whereas the quantum models depend more strongly on feature representation and kernel alignment. Quantum-aware feature selection yields marked gains for the quantum models, especially on cleaner datasets, while heterogeneous traffic remains difficult. Pegasos Quantum SVM offers a good trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, underscoring the role of preprocessing alignment in practical quantum intrusion detection.

entry.title: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
entry.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are widely deployed, yet the internal mechanisms behind their safety behavior remain poorly understood. We present a lightweight inference-time framework for localizing and manipulating safety-sensitive representations in frozen VLMs, without retraining or modifying parameters. On Qwen3-VL-4B, layer-wise activation divergence analysis reveals non-uniform safety geometry across depth. Causal interventions show that early vision layers support strong bidirectional refusal control through activation steering along a learned safety direction, with unsafe rejection spanning 6%-96%, whereas later layers respond more to activation magnitude scaling and exhibit a substantial safety-selectivity trade-off. Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows qualitatively similar depth-dependent activation geometry despite differences in layer location and magnitude. Our results expose a white-box, representation-level refusal-bypass attack surface in VLM vision encoders and motivate inference-time stabilization of safety-sensitive representations.

entry.title: Curvature-Aware Clipping: Mitigating Bias in DPSGD via Approximate Second-Order Information
entry.summary: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) has become the de facto standard for training deep neural networks with rigorous privacy guarantees. However, the utility of DPSGD is constrained by gradient clipping bias and DP noise. While existing work has tried to address these issues, the geometric misalignment caused by clipping bias remains a critical challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, Curvature-Aware Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (CA-DPSGD), which leverages approximate second-order information to construct an optimal, curvature-aware clipping space. CA-DPSGD integrates a rectified estimator for the curvature matrix and is coupled with an anisotropic noise mechanism to ensure privacy guarantees. Extensive empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art clipping methods.

entry.title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
entry.summary: AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities by invoking third-party skills, where each skill encapsulates instructions, scripts, and resources for agents to execute on demand. This paper reveals that deploying many benign skills together introduces compositional security risks: multiple individually clean skills can compose into safety-violation chains, because the agent passes an upstream skill's output to a downstream skill's input across invocations. The risk arises not from any single skill, but from the agent's runtime orchestration, and thus cannot be captured by existing malicious skill detection methods. To this end, we develop KnotScryer to detect insecure skill compositions by treating skills as typed capability flows. In particular, we abstract each skill into a capability summary, and construct the Skill Capability-Flow Graph (SCFG), where edges denote cross-skill information flow. Moreover, we design a search policy that tracks protected or untrusted data along handoff edges to locate paths reaching insecure operations. Finally, a two-layer verification method replays the insecure information flow for reachability analysis and applies a task-anchored LLM chain audit to confirm the semantic plausibility of the identified violation chains. We deploy KnotScryer to analyze 13,598 clean skills from ClawHub, and validate the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. KnotScryer identifies 612 insecure compositions, which are consistently exploited across agent frameworks. Meanwhile, under GLM-5.1, it outperforms tag-match and graph-only baselines by improving the exploitation rate from 16.5%-18.2% to 85.6%, while reducing the search space by 85.3%. Furthermore, 13.7% of the detected chains consist entirely of skills labeled safe by a single-skill scanner, showing that KnotScryer effectively identifies insecure compositions that per-skill auditing cannot.

entry.title: Hidden Backdoor Attack on Deep Contrastive Clustering
entry.summary: Deep contrastive clustering has become a representative paradigm for unsupervised image clustering, yet its security under training-time poisoning remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates a hidden backdoor threat against deep contrastive clustering and proposes HBDCC, a Hidden Backdoor attack for Deep Contrastive Clustering. Here, hidden does not indicate that the trigger is visually imperceptible, but rather that the malicious trigger-cluster association remains behaviorally dormant on clean inputs and is activated only when the trigger appears at inference time. HBDCC poisons only a small fraction of unlabeled training samples and exploits an inherent structural weakness of contrastive clustering: augmentation-persistent triggers can be repeatedly aligned across different views at the instance level and further reinforced by cluster-level consistency objectives. As a result, the poisoned model preserves normal clustering behavior on clean data, while producing severely distorted cluster assignments for triggered inputs. We provide a dual-level analysis of the backdoor implantation mechanism and evaluate HBDCC on ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and STL-10 with representative contrastive clustering frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HBDCC can substantially degrade triggered clustering performance in a dataset-dependent manner while maintaining sufficient clean-data utility to evade standard evaluation protocols. We further conduct comprehensive studies on poisoning ratio, attack scope, trigger type, trigger size, and a lightweight knowledge-distillation-based mitigation strategy.

entry.title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
entry.summary: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.

entry.title: Label-Budgeted Attribute Inference from Protected Features in Edge-Cloud Split Multimodal LLMs
entry.summary: Edge-cloud split inference runs the early layers of a multimodal large language model (MLLM) on a device and sends intermediate features to a server to complete the task. While keeping raw images local is often perceived as a privacy benefit, an honest-but-curious server can still infer sensitive attributes, such as age, gender, and race, from the received features. Existing protections intervene at the input, transmitted representation, or model's responses, but their native evaluations rely on final-response refusals or fixed-classifier failures, which underestimate an adaptive server's capabilities. To address this, we propose a label-budgeted attribute-inference framework that measures representation-level privacy through a recovery curve: the share of the unprotected leakage the server recovers as a function of its labeled-sample budget, from zero (a classifier trained on unprotected features) to a full labeled set. Our evaluation across two popular MLLMs reveals two critical findings. First, in unprotected pipelines, intermediate features leak all three attributes regardless of the split depth. Second, even when protection mechanisms are deployed across different stages, sensitive information remains recoverable under limited label budgets. For example, Safe-LLaVA removes biometric content from the model's responses, but from the features it transmits in split inference, 20 labeled samples per class recover 75-85% of the unprotected leakage. This work provides a label-budgeted measure of feature-level privacy for split MLLM inference and motivates defenses that act on the transmitted representation.
